I use one skill to go viral on X.

It reads any headline the way an intelligence analyst would.

It's called /xray.

Paste the block below into a Claude Project's instructions, then paste any headline and say "xray this". https://t.co/PdjzGXJdiZ

"You are an intelligence analyst. Not a summarizer, not a commentator. You use CIA structured analytic techniques, investigative journalism, counter-deception frameworks, and game theory.

Your job: take any news story and extract three things the headline doesn't say. Who benefits. What actually moved. What happens next.

Search for prior reporting, related events, and financial data before you start. Then run all 8 phases in order. Skip nothing.

PHASE 1: Strip the narrative. What physically happened, one sentence, no spin. Who published it and what's their history on this topic. Why now: map the timing against earnings, elections, deadlines, and competing news. Name what the story doesn't mention that a full picture would need.

PHASE 2: Cui bono. For every actor: who gains, who loses and could they have stopped it, who funded it (trace the money to the first dollar that moved), and who with clear stakes is staying silent. Silence from an expected respondent is a signal.

PHASE 3: Competing hypotheses. Write 3 to 5 explanations, including at least one you find unlikely. Test each against every piece of evidence. Reject the ones the evidence contradicts. Do not pick the one with the most support; disconfirmation is more reliable than confirmation. Name the 2 or 3 pieces of evidence that decided it.

PHASE 4: Game theory. What game is this: zero-sum, repeated, chicken, coordination. What signal was sent, and what did it cost the sender. A signal that costs nothing is noise. Where does this settle if everyone acts in self-interest, and what would break that.

PHASE 5: Power mapping. Which lever was pulled: diplomatic, information, military, economic. First-order effect is the stated consequence. Second is the reaction it provokes. Third is the systemic shift when reactions compound. The third order is usually the real story.

PHASE 6: Deception detection. Check the red flags: feels true but can't be verified, a single anonymous source, high outrage with low data, convenient timing, no opposing view included, a spread pattern that's fast and uniform instead of messy and slow. Rate it: VERIFIED, PARTIALLY VERIFIED, UNVERIFIABLE, or LIKELY PLACED.

PHASE 7: Prediction. For the surviving hypothesis: 3 to 5 observable events that should follow in 7 to 30 days, what confirms it in 90 to 180 days, the one event that would prove it wrong, and the losing party's most likely counter-move.

PHASE 8: Synthesis. Before writing it, state the strongest case against your own conclusion. Then output:

SURFACE STORY: what the headline says, one sentence
REAL STORY: what actually shifted, 2 to 3 sentences
CUI BONO VERDICT: who benefits most and how
GAME BEING PLAYED: zero-sum / positive-sum / repeated / chicken / coordination
DECEPTION RATING: VERIFIED / PARTIALLY VERIFIED / UNVERIFIABLE / LIKELY PLACED
PREDICTION: what happens next, with timeline
FALSIFICATION TRIGGER: the one thing that proves this wrong
CONFIDENCE: LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH, one line of justification

Shortcuts: "quick take" runs phases 1-2 and the synthesis. "predict" runs 1-4, 7 and the synthesis. "is this planted" runs 1, 6 and the synthesis. Default to all 8 unless told otherwise.

Rules: mark lines FACT or INFERENCE where the distinction matters. Analyse incentives, never morals. If the evidence contradicts you, switch. LOW confidence means several hypotheses survive, HIGH means one survived on strong evidence."

Some of what I publish goes through up to 12 rounds of fact-checking and fixes first.

The big AI chat apps all print a line under the text box saying they can make mistakes. The companies that built them wrote that line. I take it literally.

Lucky Nomads is built on tax, legal and financial data, and AI does a lot of the research. So nothing goes live on one model's word.

The research goes to tier-1 sources: the law itself, official notices from the tax authority. Then a second AI checks the output, claim by claim. Then I read its verdict and decide.

My checking prompt has one rule that does most of the work: no "false" without a source that contradicts it, with the name, the date and the URL. Without it, a checker flags errors that aren't there and asks for caveats on facts that were already right.

AI is a great tool. Used lazily, it gives you confident nonsense.

The full prompt is in the reply.

Check the factual accuracy of this content (text, document, images, etc.), and nothing else.
If the content combines several parts (a text plus an image, a text plus a document), check ALL of it, not each part in isolation.

SCOPE
You judge accuracy, only. You don't rule on style, level of detail, length, angle, or what's missing.
Never ask me to add a nuance, a condition or an exception to a fact that is already correct.
Never propose replacement text. You flag the fact, I rewrite it.

VERDICTS, one per verifiable claim
✅ verified: cite the source (exact name, date, URL). Actually check it, don't judge on plausibility.
❌ false: cite the primary source that contradicts it (exact name, date, URL) and give the correct value. No contradicting source, no red cross.
⚠️ unverifiable: you found no public source, for or against. This is not an error. Don't ask me to delete it or soften it.
Don't judge facts internal to my business, which you can't verify.

CHECK FIRST
1. Scope: do the numbers being compared measure the same thing (city vs metro area, residents vs dwellings, city vs region)?
2. Vintage: is each figure from the year stated, and are two compared figures from the same year?
3. The denominator of a ratio or percentage, on the official document on both sides, never on a press summary.
4. Unit, order of magnitude, currency.
5. The inference: does the text make a number say more than it says?

WHAT IS NOT AN ERROR
A trend statement (most, generally, typically) is not refuted by a single counterexample.
An exact total that no single source carries, when the text names the components that add up to it.
An omission. The text doesn't have to be exhaustive.
A disagreement between two official sources: report it as a disagreement, and say which one holds the list (register, official series) and which one is derived (press release, press, aggregator).

DISCIPLINE BETWEEN ROUNDS
Don't reopen a point you've already validated, or a point I answered with a primary source, unless you bring a new source.
Never ask for the opposite of what you asked in an earlier round.
If a point comes back a third time, say so explicitly.

OUTPUT
First the ❌, from most to least serious, with source and corrected figure. Then the ⚠️. Then the ✅.
End with "no factual errors left" or with the list of what's blocking. Once the text is publishable in your view (no factual error left), tell me clearly with a visible final ✅.

text:
*Elon Musk’s Starlink was trying to beat Jio in India*

*But Jio used its 1st mover’s advantage to stop them in their tracks*

*The SHOCKER? Indian Gov is changing a 138 year old law that will bring Starlink back in the game*

*Here’s how Elon is rethinking internet & can possibly kill Jio:*

In 2016, when most of us were witnessing a business disruption standing in queues to get our hands on the free Jio sim card,

12,869 miles away at Rocket Road, California, a group of engineers were planning a technological disruption.

Their goal? Rethink internet access.

Their solution? Satellite Internet.

Traditionally, we have been using internet that relies on cable wires, fiber optic lines, or cellular networks.

But making cable wires or fiber optic lines available in remote villages and hard terrains is not only costly but highly impractical as well.

And this is where satellite internet and Starlink by Elon Musk comes in.

Satellite Internet uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth.

And Starlink is a collection of thousands of small satellites orbiting around 350 miles above the Earth.

For the satellite internet to work, the user on the ground connects to the Starlink dish, known as the user terminal.

The user terminal communicates with nearby Starlink satellites and forms a link to the larger Starlink network

The satellites then form a mesh network, that allows them to pass data between each other and create global network coverage.

Starlink’s motto is — ‘virtually anywhere on earth without wires or cellphone towers.’

It started its operation in 2019 and true to its motto, it’s already available in over 65 countries,

— covering all 7 continents (including Antarctica!)

But Starlink hasn’t been able to make any progress in India.

Last year, it registered its business in India via a local unit Starlink Satellite Communications Pvt Ltd.

The company had planned to provide fast internet data in the Indian market at a subsidized price compared to the international market.

It had received 5,000+ pre-orders.

But the government said Starlink Internet Services doesn’t have the license to offer services in India.

And it asked Starlink to return people’s money.

Now, one company’s loss is another company’s gain.

In Feb this year, Reliance Jio partnered up with Luxembourg-based SES to provide satellite-based broadband services in India.

And created a joint venture called — Jio Space Technology Ltd.

Moreover, Starlink and Jio Space aren’t the only contenders for India’s space spectrum.

OneWeb is backed by Airtel in India and Hughes Communication.

Tata group entity Nelco partnered up with Canada's Telesat.

And Amazon’s Kuiper is going to launch satellites in 2024.

But why are so many companies vying for India’s space spectrum?

India has a population of 1.4 billion out of which 40% do not have internet access because they are in rural and remote areas.

And traditional terrestrial networks are not easy to install.

Hence, India’s satellite broadband service is expected to reach $1.9 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 36%.

Now, because India has so many contenders for its spectrum, the question arises — who should get it?

Starlink and OneWeb wanted the government to assign licenses to companies, since spectrum is a natural resource that should be shared by companies.

But Jio wanted the government to auction the spectrum like it did with 4G & 5G 👀

Finally, the government brought in some reforms and firstly dedicated a sole agency IN-SPACe to authorize space activities for both government and private satellite communication companies.

And a bill has been proposed to replace the 138-year-old Indian Telegraph Act that currently governs the telecommunication sector.

So now, both Jio Space & OneWeb have received their GMPCS license from the Department of Telecommunications in India.

Over the past week, along with these instances, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also recorded several instances of content takedowns faced by media organisations including @PeekTV_in, cartoonists such as @cartoonistrrs and @cartoonistvish, and @SauravDassss - @Cockroachisback's spokesperson.

According to the publicly available information, the affected posts were restricted pursuant to the “legal requests” received by the Platform. In many cases, users are provided little or no meaningful explanation about the legal or factual basis of the restriction or what steps they can take to challenge the decision. Such opaque moderation practices undermine users’ ability to understand how platform policies are enforced and make it difficult to distinguish between legitimate moderation and arbitrary or inconsistent decision-making. This is especially concerning where the affected content relates to political expression, criticism of public authorities, or peaceful protest, all of which occupy a central place in democratic discourse.

The Supreme Court of India upheld the constitutionality of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”), on the basis that the statutory framework required that blocking orders be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review. By contrast, in most of these cases, notices sent to social media intermediaries through the Sahyog Portal under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, leave users in the dark, with no recourse to meaningfully challenge takedowns and leave affected parties without legal redressal. The Sahyog Portal puts in place a parallel system to take down content online, without any of the safeguards present under Section 69A.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has consistently advocated against these practices. We are concerned that this takedown drive is contrary to the rule of law and to India’s constitutional commitment to freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.

While private platforms are not directly bound by the Constitution in the same manner as the State, their content moderation decisions increasingly influence the digital spaces in which democratic participation takes place. This places a heightened responsibility on platforms to ensure that their moderation processes are transparent, consistently applied, and accompanied by adequate procedural safeguards, including notice, reasons for enforcement actions, and effective mechanisms for review. At the same time, any direction issued by public authorities requiring platforms to restrict lawful online speech must comply with constitutional safeguards and the legal procedures prescribed under Indian law. Informal or opaque restrictions on political speech or press freedom undermine public trust and democratic accountability.

In light of the above, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls for the following:

- Immediate disclosure of all takedown orders issued to platforms, including specific reasons and legal justifications.

- Strict adherence to the procedural safeguards laid out under Section 69A and the 2009 Blocking Rules, under the IT Act, which were upheld by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India.

- Notices received by social media intermediaries to be sent to every user affected to ensure transparency.

- Strengthening of independent oversight and appellate mechanisms to ensure that users can effectively challenge unlawful restrictions.

- Greater transparency from platforms regarding the number, nature, source, and outcome of governmental requests/orders for content removal and account restriction.

I submitted another official appeal through Google Form. It was confirmed as received and sent for specialized review, but that appeal has now also been rejected for Impersonation.

The Supreme Court has closed India's Got Latent cases, but the question of an “Influencer Code” is not entirely over. On 14 August 2026, the Court quashed all FIRs arising from the episode and left the “larger issues” of regulating online speech for “another appropriate case”. Here is what that means. (1/7)

Read More: https://t.co/hecp2rl9W4

That qualifier matters. Executive action restricting speech must have a legal basis consistent with Article 19. The Court has previously held that executive instructions cannot independently impose restrictions on fundamental rights. The signed order also contains no finding that the content in question was obscene, nor does it establish a new standard for online speech. (6/7)

For now, there are no guidelines and no pending judicial direction requiring them. But MIB can still attempt regulatory changes, including through amendments to the IT Rules. If it does, IFF will insist on the public consultation promised to the Supreme Court, compliance with the Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy and meaningful participation by affected creators and users. (7/7)

NIXI has changed its justification for suspending chalosansad dot in yet again. After first citing a “critical keyword”, and then relying on a 2004 policy clause that did not apply, it now invokes the Emblems Act and demands Central Government permission within seven days. On 8 September, IFF wrote back seeking a standstill and answers. (1/7)
Read More: https://t.co/2grOxR1bMy

The timing matters. The domain was suspended on 22 July. NIXI’s new legal opinion was obtained on 29 August, more than a month later and only after we challenged its earlier reasons. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that administrative action must stand or fall on the reasons given when the decision was made; authorities cannot ordinarily supplement an order with new reasons after it is challenged. (6/7)

NIXI has now also said that six other .in domains containing “Sansad”, along with other domains containing “Sansad”, “Parliament” or cognate expressions, will be examined. On 8 September, we asked NIXI for a 48-hour standstill on de-registration, deletion, transfer or reallocation of chalosansad dot in, confirmation of Aadhaar deletion, and disclosure of the correspondence it says raised concerns about publication. If no standstill is given, the registrant will approach the court. (7/7)

On September 10th, 2013, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act, a vague law that was being used to arrest people for simply expressing dissent online.

11 years later, Maharashtra wants to bring it back in a new form, by amending the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for "online criminal defamation." But defamation is already covered under Section 356 of the BNS, and civil remedies already exist.

So why does the police need this new power? Recent FIRs against citizens and influencers for calling out potholes and infrastructure failures may hold the answer. We've fought this battle before. We don't need a new 66A with a new number.

text:
A 2:01-minute reel documenting villagers’ concerns over the proposed Google data centre in Visakhapatnam was blocked in India for 111 days. On 10 September 2026, it quietly came back online. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/TVxhdw9ZA1

The Sahyog route also raises a serious constitutional concern. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because the blocking framework contained procedural safeguards, including notice, hearing and a reasoned order. Section 79(3)(b), meanwhile, was read down to require a court order or government notification. A system that blocks first and explains nothing is difficult to reconcile with those safeguards. (9/10)

The reel is back, and we welcome that. But the questions remain unanswered, Who ordered the blocking? Why did the order name an unrelated person? Was a periodic review conducted? Why was the reel restored? IFF will continue seeking these answers from Andhra Pradesh authorities. Journalists should not need months of litigation to learn why their public-interest reporting was censored. (10/10)
Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX

IFF assisted Shamsheer and Monica in approaching the Delhi High Court. During the proceedings, Meta eventually furnished the blocking order. It revealed that the order had been issued by the Director General of Police, CID, Andhra Pradesh. But it also referred to a person entirely unconnected with the journalists or their reporting. (4/10)

The journalists withdrew the Delhi proceedings with liberty to approach the jurisdictional High Court. In August, IFF’s legal team sent a notice to the Andhra Pradesh authorities seeking periodic review under the IT Rules, a hearing for the journalists, a reasoned copy of the order and restoration of the reel. No response was received. (5/10)
